title: Odisha’s sweets, and the places behind them
lead: Nimapada’s Chhena Jhili, Kendrapara’s Rasabali and the other sweets that give a place another way to be remembered.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

intro.text: Ask someone about a town and a sweet may enter the conversation before a landmark. Nimapada has Chhena Jhili; Kendrapara has Rasabali. These names invite a closer look at preparation, makers and the ways food belongs to a place.

A place connection can mean several things: a making tradition, a market, a temple offering or a reputation recorded in a source. The eight sweets below form a starting collection. They are not an exhaustive list, a ranking or a claim that each sweet is made only in the named place.

paragraphs.text: Chhena Jhili brings Nimapada into the story through a syrup-soaked chhena sweet. The university teaching account describes shaping and frying the cheese mixture before soaking it in syrup. That sequence gives a visitor something to notice: the browned outside, the softer centre and how much syrup the sweet has taken in.

Uttarakhand Open University’s teaching text credits Aartabandhu Sahoo of Shyam Sundarpur, Nimapara, with starting the preparation. It is an attributed local origin account, without an independently established invention date. The 2016–17 Puri industrial profile also records the name “Nimapara Jhili”. Ask a maker how they shape it and who taught them.

Chhena Poda is a baked chhena sweet whose browned surface invites comparison with the softer cut centre. Odisha Tourism links it with Nayagarh and describes a sal-leaf-lined baking preparation. A small slice can begin a conversation about the sweetness, the crust and how a particular maker handles the baking.

Chef Michael’s 2021 contribution to Odisha Tourism describes sugar and jaggery versions and offers a chocolate adaptation. A named sweet can hold a familiar identity while a cook tries something new. When tasting, ask which sweetener was used and how it changes the baking.

photo.caption: Chhena poda photographed in Puri by Subhransuphotography, 2022. A portrait of the sweet, not a Nayagarh maker or shop.

paragraphs.text: Rasabali places fried chhena in reduced sweetened milk. The Kendrapara applicant’s 2023 account also connects it with offerings to Baladevjew. That gives the sweet a devotional setting as well as a preparation to explore; it does not establish when Rasabali was first made.

An October 2023 report names Souri Sahoo as a Rasabali maker and Baishava Panda as the makers’ association president. Their comments give the preparation named makers and a community to learn about. For a tasting, notice the fried chhena and the milk around it separately, then bring them together. Ask how the maker balances the two.

Magji’s Dhenkanal connection becomes more specific around Mandar–Sadangi. The published applicant specification describes pressed buffalo-milk cheese cooked with sugar and cardamom, then shaped by hand. The cheese, cooking and shaping give a maker several choices to explain.

In a January 2024 report, Hrushikesh Sahoo of Sadangi described Magji making by his grandfather, father and himself. That family account gives the craft a human thread without establishing the sweet’s original inventor. A conversation with a maker could begin with that handwork: how the cooked mixture is judged ready, shaped and passed from one person to another.

Korakhai offers a different texture from the milk sweets: khai brought together with sugar or jaggery, coconut and cardamom in the 2016 reported preparation. Its Old Town association includes the Lingaraj neighbourhood and an attributed temple-service tradition. A retail batch should not be assumed to be a temple offering merely because it shares the name.

Sheela Pattanayak’s 2016 report identifies Rama Sahoo with the founding of Baya Baba Kora Khai and interviews Subash Sahu, then owner of Jagat Bikhyat Korakhai. A separate official town table lists Korakhai among Bhubaneswar’s manufactured and outward-traded goods for 1999. These are dated traces of people and commerce, not current shop recommendations.

Pahala and Salepur deserve separate places in a rasagola introduction. Argho Mukherjee’s account of a 2019 visit describes Pahala’s roadside sweet market between Bhubaneswar and Cuttack and also names Salepur’s rasagola tradition. The connection is to making and selling communities; it does not make the two places interchangeable or establish a single origin.

Rasagola also has a Puri ritual connection: OSIC’s 2019 account describes the sweet’s offering to Lakshmi on Jagannath’s behalf at Niladri Bije. Ritual, a regional product identity and a local market tell different parts of the story. Ask a maker what distinguishes their preparation and who taught them, while keeping a family’s account distinct from a history of every rasagola.

photo.caption: Pahala rasagola photographed by Archbik; uploaded 2010, capture date unconfirmed. This is not a photograph of Salepur’s preparation.

paragraphs.text: Puri’s Khaja shifts attention from cheese to layers. Odisha Tourism describes a crisp, layered fried sweet lightly soaked in sugar syrup, and places Khaja within the state’s temple-offering traditions. Look at the broken edge before tasting: the layers are part of the preparation to ask about.

At a sweet shop, ask about the flour, folding, frying and syrup used in that batch. If you encounter Khaja as a temple offering, learn about that setting too: the preparation and the occasion both deserve attention.

Bhadrak’s district cultural account names Palua Ladu among its recognised sweets, alongside Chena Mudki. This is a useful starting point for learning the district through its food. A fuller record would include the maker’s own name for the sweet, its ingredients and the work that gives it its texture.

In his 2020 travel account hosted by Odisha Tourism, Argho Mukherjee describes a Palua Ladoo preparation using semolina, wheat flour, arrowroot and sugar. Treat that as the contributor’s description, not an agreed formula for every Bhadrak maker. Asking a maker what palua means in their preparation and how the mixture is worked would make a useful next record.

closing.text: Choose a sweet you want to understand rather than trying to finish the list. Ask its local name, how it was made, which ingredients it contains and how the maker recommends storing and carrying that particular batch. Confirm price and portion before buying; this collection supplies no verified current shop list or storage duration.

If you record a conversation or photograph the making, ask permission and keep the maker’s name with their account. A date, a place and a specific preparation make a more useful memory than an unqualified claim about the oldest or best sweet.

There is more to document. Sambalpur’s Sarsatia is a strong next candidate: Odisha Tourism links the fine-stranded sweet with the city, rice flour and Ganjeer sap. Its summary and detailed preparation differ, so it remains a further-research lead outside this first collection.
